rows.selection_reason: With no prior experiments completed, the highest-priority question is establishing a clean, interpretable performance baseline. config_005 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest possible configuration: no learned encoder, no aggregation, no fusion. It will (1) provide a reference accuracy/F1 for the task using only transcriptomic data with a standard linear reduction, (2) serve as the anchor against which all future multimodal, multiprofile, or learned-encoder experiments can be compared to isolate the marginal contribution of each added design element, and (3) be fast to train, preserving budget for subsequent experiments. Starting here allows a systematic one-factor-at-a-time exploration: I can next vary the RNA encoder (scvi_n200, scgpt), add image modality, switch to multiprofile, or change aggregation/fusion, each time attributing performance shifts to a single change. This is the most information-efficient first step under a limited budget.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_005: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), establishing a weak RNA-only baseline. The central uncertainty is whether the image modality adds any predictive value, which is the core question of a multimodal study. Question tested: config_023 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion) keeps the profile setting and RNA encoder identical to the baseline and introduces only the image encoder and the necessary fusion step. This isolates the contribution of the image modality with minimal confounding. Why best next step: Under a tight budget, directly comparing a multimodal model to the existing RNA-only baseline (same profile, same RNA encoder) gives the cleanest signal on whether adding a second modality is worthwhile. If config_023 substantially exceeds 0.485, we validate the multimodal direction and can then explore encoder/aggregation/fusion variants; if it does not, we learn early that the image modality or simple concat fusion is not the right lever, redirecting effort toward RNA encoder or profile choices. This is more informative than testing image-only (which would not tell us whether fusion works) or jumping to a complex multiprofile multimodal config (which would change too many variables at once).

Evidence: config_023 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved 0.535 acc / 0.519 F1, a clear ~5-point improvement over the rna_only baseline (config_005: 0.485/0.464), confirming that the image modality with ViT-L and concat fusion is beneficial. The largest untested design axis is whether moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with aggregation can further improve performance. Question: Does multiprofile + avgpool aggregation, while holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), and fusion (concat) constant, improve over the singleprofile baseline? Why this experiment: config_003 is the minimal, clean extension of config_023 along the profile/aggregation axis, changing only profile_setting (single→multi) and adding avgpool aggregation. This isolates the multiprofile effect before introducing the more complex transformer aggregation or a different fusion strategy. If multiprofile+avgpool helps, we can then test transformer aggregation (config_017) or weighted fusion; if it does not, we save budget by avoiding more complex aggregation variants. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.629 acc, a large jump over config_023 (same but singleprofile, 0.535), indicating that multiprofile aggregation is a critical design choice. The specific aggregation method (avgpool) has not been stress-tested. Question: Does transformer-based aggregation outperform simple average pooling for combining multiple profiles, while holding all other variables (pca_n2000, ViT-L, concat fusion) constant? Why this is best: config_017 is a clean single-variable ablation against the current best (config_003), isolating the aggregation effect. If transformer helps, it identifies a further improvement axis; if avgpool is sufficient, it confirms a simpler design and redirects budget toward other dimensions (fusion type, encoder choice). This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

All four completed experiments used concat fusion, so the effect of weighted fusion remains entirely untested. config_003 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.629 acc, and config_022 is identical except for switching fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates a single design variable (fusion strategy) against the strongest known baseline, directly testing whether learned channel weighting improves over simple concatenation. Under a tight budget, this is the highest-information single-variable extension: if weighted fusion helps, it identifies a new lever to exploit across other encoders/aggregations; if it does not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects budget toward untested encoders (scvi_n200, scgpt) or image backbones (resnet50).

The current best (config_022: pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.635 acc / 0.618 F1. All completed experiments use PCA as the RNA encoder, leaving the RNA representation choice entirely unexplored. config_046 is a single-variable change from the current best, swapping pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 while holding image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (avgpool), fusion (weighted), and profile setting (multiprofile) constant. This directly tests whether a learned nonlinear RNA latent (scVI) captures biological structure that PCA misses, which is a critical design axis given that the RNA modality is the primary biological signal. If scvi_n200 improves performance, it identifies RNA encoder quality as a lever for further gains; if it does not, it confirms PCA sufficiency and redirects budget toward other dimensions (e.g., image encoder or fusion). This is the highest-information single experiment available under the limited budget.

The RNA encoder is clearly the most impactful design choice: switching from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (config_022→config_046, all else identical) yielded the largest single improvement in the study (+7.1% accuracy, 0.635→0.706). However, we have not yet tested the third available learned encoder, scgpt. Config_014 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is an exact single-variable swap against our current best (config_046), isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding image encoder, aggregation, fusion, and profile setting constant. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the superior learned representation and lets us redirect remaining budget to other dimensions (e.g., aggregation or image encoder). Under a limited budget, resolving uncertainty on the highest-leverage design axis with a clean controlled comparison is the most efficient use of the next experiment.

Evidence: scvi_n200 dramatically outperforms pca_n2000 (+0.071 acc) and scgpt (+0.164 acc) under identical multimodal/multiprofile/vit_l/avgpool/weighted settings (config_046: 0.706 vs config_022: 0.635 vs config_014: 0.542). However, we have no rna_only baseline with scvi_n200 and multiprofile, so we cannot determine how much of the 0.706 performance is driven by the RNA encoder alone versus the image modality. Question: config_012 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) isolates the RNA contribution by removing the image modality while keeping the best-known RNA encoder and profile setting. Why this is the best next experiment: The gap between rna_only/scvi_n200/multiprofile and the current best (config_046) directly quantifies the image modality's marginal contribution. If the gap is small (<0.03), future effort should focus on RNA encoder refinement; if large (>0.08), image encoder choice and fusion strategy become critical levers. This single ablation resolves a major source of uncertainty that would otherwise misdirect subsequent experiments, making it more informative than a marginal aggregation or fusion swap on the already-strong config_046.

Evidence: config_046 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the best result at 0.706 acc. The only prior evidence on aggregation (avgpool vs. transformer) comes from pca_n2000, where avgpool outperformed transformer (0.629 vs 0.599, configs 003 vs 017). However, scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different learned, nonlinear, low-dimensional representation, so the aggregation ranking may not transfer. Question: config_006 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while keeping scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, and weighted fusion fixed, directly testing whether transformer aggregation can better model interactions in the scvi latent space. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a single-variable, clean comparison against the current best (config_046), it resolves the most important unresolved design question (aggregation) in the context of the dominant RNA encoder, and it could either confirm that avgpool is robustly superior or uncover a further performance gain—both outcomes are highly informative under a limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_006: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, acc=0.725) has only been tested with imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder. All top-performing multimodal configs use this specific encoder, leaving the image encoder architecture as an unexplored critical design dimension in the high-performing regime. Config_038 makes a single-variable change (imagenet_vit_l → resnet50) from config_006, cleanly isolating the effect of image encoder choice. If resnet50 performs comparably, the image modality contribution is robust to architecture and we can focus optimization on other axes; if it drops significantly, it confirms imagenet_vit_l is essential and the gap informs how much the image representation contributes. This is the best use of the next experiment because it tests the least-resolved design choice in the current best-performing region, provides actionable guidance for practical deployment (lighter encoder), and is a controlled single-variable comparison rather than a multi-factor change.
